title: From One Cell to an Organism

concepts.title: The Central Question
concepts.contentHtml:
A fertilized egg is a single cell. Forty weeks later it's a baby with ~10¹³ cells, organized into hundreds of cell types and dozens of organs. How?

Every cell shares the same DNA. Differential gene expression creates different cell types: a neuron transcribes different genes than a muscle cell, even from identical genomes.

Position matters. Cells acquire identity from their location, communicating with neighbors. Development is a vast spatial-temporal pattern of gene expression unfolding from molecular signals.

concepts.title: Cleavage and Blastula
concepts.contentHtml:
Right after fertilization, the zygote divides rapidly without growing — cleavage. Cells become smaller and more numerous; cell cycle is short.

By ~100 cells, the embryo is a hollow ball — blastula (or blastocyst in mammals). Outer cells will form the placenta; inner cell mass will form the embryo proper.

Stem cell biology was largely born from understanding the inner cell mass — pluripotent cells that can become any cell type.

concepts.title: Gastrulation
concepts.contentHtml:
Gastrulation establishes the three germ layers: ectoderm (skin and nervous system), mesoderm (muscle, bone, blood, kidneys), endoderm (gut and lungs).

Cells migrate dramatically — folding and invaginating into the embryo. 'It is not birth, marriage, or death, but gastrulation, which is truly the most important time in your life' — Lewis Wolpert.

Once germ layers are set, the body plan unfolds rapidly. Most major organ rudiments appear in the first 8 weeks of human development.

title: Morphogens & Pattern Formation
description: How cells know where they are

concepts.title: The Morphogen Concept
concepts.contentHtml:
A morphogen is a signaling molecule that diffuses across a tissue, forming a concentration gradient. Cells respond to different concentrations differently — high → fate A, medium → fate B, low → fate C.

Lewis Wolpert's French flag model (1969) was the conceptual cornerstone: a single gradient can create multiple sharp domains based on threshold responses.

Famous examples: Bicoid in Drosophila (anterior-posterior axis), Sonic hedgehog (Shh) in vertebrate limb and neural tube, Wnt and BMP in many tissues.

concepts.title: Hox Genes
concepts.contentHtml:
The Hox genes are a conserved family of master regulators that specify body-plan identity along the anterior-posterior axis. Each Hox gene is expressed in a specific region; different combinations specify different segments.

The same Hox genes — in roughly the same order on the chromosome — pattern the body of fruit flies, frogs, mice, and humans. Spectacular conservation across ~600 million years of animal evolution.

Mutations in Hox genes produce dramatic 'homeotic transformations' — antennae replaced by legs in fruit flies; cervical vertebrae transformed into thoracic in mice.

concepts.title: Reaction-Diffusion & Self-Organization
concepts.contentHtml:
Alan Turing (1952) showed that simple reaction-diffusion equations can spontaneously generate periodic patterns — stripes, spots, hexagonal patches. Turing patterns.

Animal coat patterns (zebra stripes, leopard spots), digit spacing, hair-follicle distribution all show reaction-diffusion signatures. Recent experiments confirm Turing-mechanism contributions.

Beautiful spatial structure can emerge from simple chemical interactions — no master plan needed. Development is partly self-organization.

concepts.title: Potency
concepts.contentHtml:
Cells differ in potency — the range of cell types they can become.

• Totipotent: the zygote and early blastomeres — can form an entire organism, including extra-embryonic tissues.
• Pluripotent: inner cell mass / embryonic stem cells — can form any embryonic cell type but not placenta.
• Multipotent: adult stem cells (e.g., hematopoietic) — can form a limited set of related cell types.
• Unipotent: only one cell type (e.g., muscle satellite cells).

concepts.title: Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs)
concepts.contentHtml:
Shinya Yamanaka's 2006 work showed that just four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc) can reprogram an adult cell to pluripotency — making induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).

Yamanaka shared the 2012 Medicine Nobel. iPSCs sidestep the ethical concerns of embryonic stem cells and can be derived from a patient's own cells.

iPSCs are now used to model diseases in vitro (patient-specific neurons for ALS, Parkinson's), to test drugs, and (increasingly) for cell-based therapies.

concepts.title: Adult Stem Cells & Tissue Renewal
concepts.contentHtml:
Adult bodies maintain stem-cell pools to replace cells throughout life. Hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow generate ~10¹¹ blood cells per day. Intestinal crypt stem cells replenish the gut lining every few days. Hair follicle stem cells regenerate hair.

Loss of stem-cell function contributes to aging. Activation of stem-cell programs is also a feature of cancer — many tumors maintain a stem-like population that resists treatment.

Therapeutic applications: bone-marrow transplants exploit hematopoietic stem cells; corneal limbal stem-cell transplants treat blindness; mesenchymal stem-cell therapies are explored for many diseases.

concepts.title: The Heart
concepts.contentHtml:
The heart is the first organ to form and function — a remarkable engineering feat. Cardiac progenitors from mesoderm migrate, fold, loop, and partition into chambers. Beating begins at ~22 days in human embryos.

Congenital heart defects affect ~1% of births. Many are now surgically correctable; some are detected by prenatal ultrasound.

Stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes are being explored for heart-failure repair. Engineered cardiac patches and bioprinted tissue are research-stage but advancing.

concepts.title: The Nervous System
concepts.contentHtml:
Neural induction transforms part of the ectoderm into neural plate, which folds into the neural tube — the precursor of brain and spinal cord. The brain develops from anterior expansions of this tube.

~250,000 neurons per minute are generated during peak human brain development. Neurons migrate from where they're born to their final positions, then extend axons to connect with targets.

Neural development errors cause many disorders: spina bifida (failed neural tube closure), microcephaly, lissencephaly. Folate supplementation during pregnancy prevents many of these.

concepts.title: Limb Development
concepts.contentHtml:
Limbs sprout from the body wall as limb buds. Three signaling centers organize them: AER (apical ectodermal ridge — drives elongation via FGFs), ZPA (zone of polarizing activity — Sonic hedgehog gradient sets thumb-pinky axis), and dorsal-ventral signals (Wnt7a).

Hand-foot differences emerge from positional signals. Disrupting these signals produces extra digits, missing digits, or duplications.

This is among the best-studied morphogenetic processes — model for understanding signal integration in development.

title: Regeneration & Frontiers
description: Why some animals can regrow what we cannot

concepts.title: Regeneration in the Animal Kingdom
concepts.contentHtml:
Some animals regenerate spectacularly. Planarians (flatworms) can regenerate from a tiny piece — including head from tail. Axolotls regrow limbs, tails, even portions of heart and brain. Zebrafish regrow fins, retinas, hearts.

Mammals are mostly poor regenerators. Liver is the main exception — partial hepatectomy regenerates remarkably. Skin and gut renew constantly. But amputated limbs don't regrow.

Why is unclear. Trade-offs with cancer suppression, with developmental robustness, or with mammal-specific physiology have all been proposed.

concepts.title: Tissue Engineering & Organoids
concepts.contentHtml:
Organoids are 3D miniature organs grown from stem cells in a dish. Brain organoids, liver organoids, intestinal organoids, kidney organoids — many are now possible. They model disease, screen drugs, and explore development in ways earlier 2D culture couldn't.

Tissue engineering on scaffolds (collagen, decellularized organ matrix) aims to grow transplantable tissue. Engineered tracheas and bladders have been transplanted; engineered hearts remain experimental.

3D bioprinting deposits cells layer by layer in custom geometries. Vasculature — keeping cells alive in thick tissues — remains a major hurdle.

concepts.title: Frontiers in Developmental Biology
concepts.contentHtml:
Single-cell sequencing now traces the developmental lineage of every cell, revealing progenitor populations and their differentiation paths. Cell atlases of mouse, human, and dozens of other species are being assembled.

Live imaging with light-sheet microscopy follows development in real time — entire embryos can be tracked cell by cell from fertilization to organism.

Synthetic embryology: stem cells self-organize into embryo-like structures (blastoids, gastruloids) — modeling early development without using actual embryos. Ethical and regulatory frameworks are evolving.
